title: The Portrait of Vessel Farm
premise: Rafael Villalobos returns to Vessel Farm to bury her twin brother Rafael—born with the same name, the sibling no one outside the family ever knew existed—and finds her childhood imaginary friend, Marisol, waiting on the porch, unchanged since 1974. As Rafael documents the farm's decaying rooms and her family's careful silences, she learns that 'Rafael' was never a person but a vessel: every generation, something in the well takes one child and leaves a hollow copy behind. To survive what is rising again, she must return the stolen name—the true one buried under the orchard—to the well before it refills, choosing truth over the loyalty that kept her family alive. In the end she gives back what was taken, loses the brother-shaped memory she loved, and gains a found family of witnesses who finally say the real names out loud.
about_author: O. M. Montrose is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing abandoned homesteads across the American Southwest before turning to fiction. They write horror about inheritance, paperwork, and the things families agree not to see.

chapters.title: The Wrong Sibling
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. She arrives at Vessel Farm with a coffin, a camera, and a notebook, documenting the funeral arrangements for a brother whose death certificate lists her own birthdate. The town sends casseroles and avoids eye contact. Emotional beat: grief braided with the uncanny suspicion that she is mourning herself.

chapters.title: Marisol on the Porch
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. At dusk she finds Marisol—her childhood imaginary friend—sitting on the porch swing, aged not a day, greeting her by a name Rafael hasn't heard since 1974. Marisol says only: 'You came back late.' Emotional beat: terror and longing colliding; documentation begins to feel like prayer.

chapters.title: Inventory of Rooms
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. She photographs every room, cataloguing the house's deliberate erasures: a bedroom stripped to wallpaper ghosts, two toothbrushes in a 1974 cup, a ledger of names crossed out. Her aunt Consuelo watches from the stairs and says nothing. Emotional beat: the house as a confession no one will read aloud.

chapters.title: What Aunt Consuelo Admits
chapters.summary: Consuelo's POV. Over cold coffee, she admits there were always two children born to the Villaloboses—one given to the well, one kept. She refuses to say which Rafael is. Emotional beat: loyalty as a cage; love expressed as silence.

chapters.title: The Ledger of Taken Names
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. In the cellar she finds the family ledger going back to 1911: pairs of names per generation, one struck through. The last entry, 1974, reads 'Rafael' twice, neither crossed out. Emotional beat: dread sharpening into purpose; the archive becomes an accusation.

chapters.title: Marisol Remembers Water
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV (strange, dreamlike). She recalls the year of the taking from below—not as victim but as witness, the thing the taken children become. She describes the well refilling on a schedule, and how long the current vessel has been leaking. Emotional beat: sympathy for the monster; hunger disguised as friendship.

chapters.title: Neighbors Who Look Away
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. She interviews the town: the feed store owner whose sister 'moved away' in 1963, the priest who keeps a locked baptismal record. Everyone knows; everyone chose survival over truth. Emotional beat: loneliness of the only person willing to look.

chapters.title: The Orchard Dig
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. Following ledger marginalia, she digs beneath the oldest apple tree and uncovers a tin box: a hospital bracelet, a lock of hair, and a christening certificate for 'Soledad Villalobos, 1974.' Emotional beat: the ground gives up its first truth; her hands shake as she documents it.

chapters.title: Consuelo Breaks
chapters.summary: Consuelo's POV. Confronted with the box, she confesses: the well took Soledad, and the family gave the surviving twin both names to confuse it. It worked for fifty years. It is working less well now. Emotional beat: guilt finally spoken; relief that curdles into fear.

chapters.title: The Well Begins to Fill
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. The dry well on the back acre seeps black water overnight; frogs with human teeth gather at its lip. Marisol grows more solid, more insistent: 'Bring me my name and I'll let you keep yours.' Emotional beat: deadline made physical; the price of survival comes due.

chapters.title: Photographs That Move
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. Reviewing her documentation, she finds images shifting between prints—the empty bedroom occupied by a small figure, the porch swing holding two. Her records, her prayers, are being answered by something reading along. Emotional beat: the archive turns hostile; faith weaponized.

chapters.title: The Cousin Who Stayed
chapters.summary: New character Tomás's POV. A cousin who never left the county arrives uninvited, having watched the farm his whole life. He offers help and his grandmother's stories: the well doesn't want a name, it wants a keeper. Emotional beat: found family forming out of shared witness.

chapters.title: Baptismal Records
chapters.summary: Rafael and Tomás's alternating POV. They persuade the dying old priest to open the locked register: Soledad was baptized the day she vanished; 'Rafael' never was. Unnamed, the surviving twin was never fully claimed by either world. Emotional beat: bureaucratic horror; paperwork as exorcism.

chapters.title: Marisol's Bargain
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. She lays out terms at the well's edge: return the name Soledad to the water, and the refill stops—but the taken are never returned, only released. Rafael must decide whether truth is worth a grief that changes shape. Emotional beat: temptation framed as mercy.

chapters.title: Night of the Refill
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. The well rises past its stones; water climbs the farmhouse walls in the dark, filling rooms with the sound of a drowned nursery. Consuelo nearly walks into it, called by Soledad's voice. Rafael drags her back. Emotional beat: survival instinct versus the seduction of reunion.

chapters.title: Choosing Truth
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. At dawn she gathers the family, the cousin, the priest's register, and reads every taken name aloud—including her own double identity—breaking the fifty-year pact of silence. The house groans; Marisol screams. Emotional beat: loyalty to the dead surrendered to loyalty to the living.

chapters.title: Returning What Was Taken
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. At the well she returns the tin box, the certificate, the name Soledad, speaking it into the black water. The refill halts mid-inch. Marisol, flickering, asks if Rafael will forget her too. Emotional beat: sacrifice without rescue; the cost paid in full.

chapters.title: What the Well Keeps
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV, final time. Released, she becomes the sum of every taken child, briefly visible as many small figures holding hands before the water stills forever. She thanks Rafael for saying the names. Emotional beat: terrible grace; the monster revealed as the mourned.

chapters.title: The Funeral, Corrected
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. They rebury the coffin under the right name, with the whole town watching—witnesses now, not accomplices. Consuelo weeps openly for the first time in fifty years. Emotional beat: public truth as communal healing; grief finally allowed its real object.

chapters.title: Closing the Ledger
chapters.summary: Tomás's POV. He helps Rafael complete the final inventory: rooms photographed, names restored, the ledger annotated so no future Villalobos inherits the silence. The well is capped in concrete and planted over with marigolds. Emotional beat: documentation fulfilled as prayer answered.

chapters.title: Found Family
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. Weeks later, the farm fills with cousins, neighbors, and strangers drawn by the story—people who choose to stay and remember together. Rafael teaches them the archive, the rituals, the names. Emotional beat: warmth after horror; belonging built deliberately, not inherited.

chapters.title: The Portrait of Vessel Farm
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV, coda. She hangs a commissioned portrait of the farmhouse in the front hall—and paints into its background, faintly, every taken child standing on the porch, present and named. On quiet evenings she swears the figures smile. Emotional beat: haunted peace; memory chosen over forgetting, and the story sealed shut.
